title: What prayer is
hookLine: less about getting words right, more like talking and listening to someone who's already there

cards: A hospital waiting room. A plane in bad turbulence. The night before the results come back.
Please. Just, please. Sometimes it comes out before anyone decides to say it, even from people who'd never call themselves religious.
And some who've gone to church their whole lives say prayer is the part they feel worst at: wrong words, wrong posture, wandering mind, nothing happening.
For the next few weeks, this path turns from stories to practices, the things Christians actually do, day to day, starting with the most basic. What is prayer, actually?

teach.b: English pray comes, through old French, from the Latin precari: to ask, to beg. Asking is part of it. But the Christian tradition keeps insisting prayer is bigger than a request line.
It's talking and listening, to someone who, Christians say, is already there before you start. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says don't pray to be seen.
"But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." A closet: a small, private room.
Don't pile up words, either, thinking more words get you heard, "for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." So why pray at all, if God already knows?
Christians have given many answers, but a common one: prayer isn't about informing God. It's about being with him. That's the talking half.
The listening half is just as old.
In the Hebrew Bible, a boy named Samuel keeps hearing his name called in the night, and an old priest teaches him what to say: "Speak; for thy servant heareth."
The prophet Elijah looks for God in a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, and finds him instead in a still small voice. Christians pray in many ways.
Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran Christians often use set prayers, words handed down for centuries. Many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians pray freely, in their own words.
Quakers often wait together in silence. The next days will try several. Under all of them is one simple shape.

how: Christians pray alone and together: many use set prayers such as the Lord's Prayer and the prayers of their church's liturgy, many pray in their own words, and some wait in silence. Many pray at set times, such as morning, evening and before meals.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: prayer means getting the words exactly right
Jesus warns against piling up words: your Father knows what you need before you ask.
listening is an old part of Christian prayer
Samuel's speak; for thy servant heareth, and Elijah's still small voice, come from the Hebrew Bible.
all Christians pray the same way
many use set prayers, many pray in their own words, and Quakers often wait together in silence.

games.q: you're young Samuel. a voice keeps calling your name in the night. the old priest tells you what to say next time. what is it?
o: who are you, and what do you want?
games.why: Samuel says: speak; for thy servant heareth. a prayer that is almost all listening.

practice: If you pray, say one honest sentence to God; if you don't, say it into the quiet: what you're grateful for, afraid of, or need. Then stop and listen for a minute.
You may hear only your breath and the room; that's fine, listening is the practice, not hearing.

wordCard.voice: Prayer. From the Latin for asking, and for Christians something wider: talking and listening to God. Camp three's first word.

orig.note: Greek: prayer, the New Testament's usual word, built from euche, a wish or vow, turned toward God.
